name: Liam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dr Weber. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Call me Liam, please, I still flinch at Dr Weber. I'm in my first year as a qualified family doctor at Millbrook Health Centre, which is a public clinic in an old mill town where half the patients used to work at the dye works. I get in at quarter to eight, read through blood results before the phones open, and then it's twelve-minute appointments until lunch. I always run late, usually by about forty minutes by eleven, because I'm still slower than the senior doctors at sorting the important from the noise.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, honestly. There's an old man, a retired dye worker, who brings me a bag of plums from his allotment every August, and I'd do the job for that alone. What wears me out is the typing: referral letters, sick notes, forms for housing, and the notes for every single visit, which I finish at home at nine at night while my partner Noor marks her Year 4 spelling tests next to me. And the money, which nobody believes, because I'm a doctor. Between my student loan and our rent on Station Road, we have about three weeks of cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I can picture that pretty easily, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the staff room: good, now can we talk about the real problems. The health centre is short two doctors, the waiting list for physio is five months, and the building leaks when it rains. AI flopping doesn't fix any of that, and I'd post something like that if I posted anything, which I mostly don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I'm a doctor with a bank balance that wouldn't cover one month's rent, and AI flopping doesn't fix that. The typing at nine at night would still be there too, which is the bit I was secretly hoping a machine would take off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am and finish my family medicine training, which is three more years. The one thing I'd do is put £100 a month aside from January, into a separate account so I can't touch it, because three weeks of savings scares me more than any robot. And I'd keep using the note-drafting tool the health trust trialled last spring when it's switched on, since even a small time-saver gets me home earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary, I suppose. A low hum of worry that has nothing to do with AI, more about the overdraft and whether Noor and I can ever afford to buy somewhere. It's not panic, it's just there in the background every month when the rent goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the note-drafting tool. How did that trial go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was patchy. It wrote a decent summary of a chest infection visit but once put down that a woman's mother had diabetes when it was her aunt, and I only caught it because the patient was sitting right there. So I used it now and then, checked every line, and it maybe saved me twenty minutes a day. Twenty minutes is twenty minutes, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes for years, what does the next stretch look like for you and Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three more years of training on trainee pay, a bit more each year, and the same flat. We'd talked about moving closer to Noor's school but rents there are higher. If nothing changes, I'm honestly worried about the money more than the job, because there are only two other clinics within an hour and both have waiting lists for doctors' posts too.

say: I'd say AI flopping changes nothing about the **real problems**: two missing doctors and five-month physio waits.
I'd mostly stay quiet online and say the same thing in the **staff room**.
think: I'm quietly **disappointed**, because I hoped a machine would take the evening typing off me.
My real worry is **money**, with about three weeks of savings and a student loan.
do: Finish my **three years** of family medicine training at Millbrook Health Centre as planned.
Put **£100 a month** into a separate savings account from January.
Use the trust's **note-drafting tool** when it's on, checking every line.
feel: A **low hum** of money worry that has nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: I'm a doctor with a bank balance that wouldn't cover one month's rent, and AI flopping doesn't fix that.
fieldNote: His job feels **safe** to him; the pressure he names is **thin savings** and student debt.
He already trialled an AI note tool and found a real **error** about a family history.
Only **two other clinics** within an hour, so staying put is less a choice than a fact.
Says he doesn't post online; his public voice is the **staff room**.

steps.text: Finish the three years of family medicine training at Millbrook
Move £100 a month into a locked savings account from January
Use the trust's note-drafting tool and check every line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's closer to home. That's roughly what the health trust's newsletters already sound like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules before the software goes in, and the doctors' union needs a seat at the table. Online, I'd share the union's line about patient safety and staffing, because that's what I believe. I'd say AI writing letters is fine, AI deciding who gets an appointment is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if software writes the referral letters, the health trust will ask why Millbrook needs two junior doctors. I'm the slow one, so I know whose name comes up. The thinking parts of my day, the triage calls and the letters and the results, are maybe half of it, and that's the half they'd automate first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union branch meeting, which I currently skip because I'm too tired, and push for an agreement on how AI gets used. I'd ask Dr Okafor, our lead doctor, to put me forward for the AI pilot, because if it's coming I'd rather understand it than be replaced by it. And I'd cut our takeaways and the gym, maybe £80 a month, so the savings grow faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. I spent six years and a lot of debt getting here, and the idea that I'd be the one they don't need feels unfair. But there's also some time, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat, our receptionist, more than me. She's been answering the phones for twenty-two years and knows every family in town, and the card literally says answering customers. If the trust brings in an AI phone line, Pat goes first, and the patients lose the one person who knows whose husband just died.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather understand AI than be replaced by it, but you also said you'd fight it through the union. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, and I don't think that's a contradiction. I'd use the tools in my own work and still fight for rules about how the trust uses them on staff and patients. A union isn't anti-machine, it's anti being treated like a spare part.

say: I'd say the doctors' **union** needs a seat at the table before software goes in.
AI writing letters is fine, but AI deciding **who gets seen** is not.
think: The trust will ask why the centre needs **two junior doctors**, and I'm the slow one.
About **half my day** is letters, triage calls and results, the part AI takes first.
do: Go to every **union branch** meeting and push for a written agreement on AI use.
Ask Dr Okafor to put me on the **AI pilot** at the health centre.
Cut takeaways and the gym to save about **£80 a month**.
feel: A **tight chest**, because six years and the debt might end with being surplus.
Some **relief** that there's still time to adjust.
S1.quote: If software writes the referral letters, the health trust will ask why Millbrook needs two junior doctors. I'm the slow one, so I know whose name comes up.
fieldNote: He sees his **post**, not the profession, as the thing at risk, because he's junior and slow.
Worries more about the **receptionist** than himself, which says a lot about his values.
Resolves the union versus AI tension calmly: use the tools, **fight for rules**.
Willing to move once something is proven, but **cautious** about being first.

steps.text: Attend every doctors' union branch meeting and push for an AI agreement
Ask Dr Okafor for a place on the trust's AI pilot
Drop takeaways and the gym to save about £80 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I even finish my training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this needs governments to act now, not in five years: protect patients, protect jobs, and tax the companies making the money. I'd be at whatever rally the union called, probably outside the town hall. I'd also say doctors aren't the ones who'll suffer most, the receptionists and the call-centre people will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a clinic with AGI only needs a couple of doctors to sign things off and do the hands-on bits. I'm a trainee with three weeks of savings, so I'd be out before the robots even show up in 2031. The hands-on stuff, listening to chests and feeling tummies, buys some doctors three years, but they'd keep the experienced ones for that, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Noor the first weekend and work out what we live on if I'm cut to part-time or let go. I'd look for anything hands-on I could add fast, like a minor surgery course or joint injections, because that's the part a machine can't do until 2031. And I'd sign us up for the union's legal help and hardship fund, and talk to my parents about moving back into their spare room if it comes to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the moment in the exam hall when you turn the page and don't recognise any of the questions. I'd be furious too, at the companies and at a government that let it happen with no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first, if your income drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The student loan repayments stop on their own if my income drops, so that's not the one. The rent is £740 and we can't miss that, so it'd be the car, a 2014 hatchback I'd sell, and Noor's evening course. That's the bit that makes me angriest, that her plans would go first because of my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the man with the plums, if he asked whether you'd still be his doctor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth, that I don't know. I'd say a machine might look at his blood results, but I'd fight to be the one who checks his feet and asks about his wife. Then I'd probably go and sit in my car for five minutes.

say: I'd say governments must act **now**: protect patients and jobs, and **tax** the companies.
I'd point out that **receptionists** and call-centre staff will suffer before doctors do.
think: A clinic with AGI needs only a few doctors to **sign off** results and examine people.
As a trainee with **three weeks** of savings, I'd be cut before the robots arrive in 2031.
do: Work out with Noor what we live on if I'm **part-time** or let go.
Take a fast **minor surgery** or joint injection course, the hands-on work machines can't do yet.
Sign up for the union's **hardship fund** and ask my parents about their spare room.
feel: **Sick**, like turning an exam page and recognising nothing.
**Furious** at the companies and at a government with no plan.
S2.quote: I'm a trainee with three weeks of savings, so I'd be out before the robots even show up in 2031.
fieldNote: He clearly understood the **3-year gap** before robots, and decided it protects senior doctors, not him.
Turned straight to **hands-on skills** as the place to hide for those three years.
Biggest anger was that **Noor's plans** would be cut first because of his job.
Political response is strong and immediate: **rallies**, taxes, union legal help.

steps.text: Draw up a part-time budget with Noor in the first weekend
Book a minor surgery and joint injection course within months
Join the union rally and sign up for its hardship fund
Ask his parents about moving into their spare room if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So I'd be just qualified as a full family doctor when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if anyone actually starts planning. At work I'd push the union to get a deal now on retraining and pay protection, while there's still bargaining power. Online I'd probably share the same thing, maybe write to our local MP for the first time in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's strange, because I'd finish training in 2029 and get two years as a proper family doctor before AGI. I'd have a family medicine qualification that's worth less right after I get it. But I'd also be experienced enough by then that I might be one of the doctors they keep for the hands-on work until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the training, no question, and then aim my last year at hands-on skills: coils and implants, minor surgery, home visits to frail patients. I'd also save harder, maybe £200 a month once my pay goes up in 2027, so we've got three months by the time it arrives. And I'd write to our MP and ask what the plan is for health workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the two-year one, more like a constant worry I'd carry around. There's time, but it's the kind of time that goes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared to the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd panic and grab whatever course I could. With five, I'd pick properly, maybe do a diploma in caring for older people, because the town is old and that work is mostly about touch, trust and home visits. I'd also have time to try the AI tools seriously and figure out where they're wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change any plans with Noor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about trying for a baby in about four years. In this picture I'd want to wait until we see what 2031 does to my job, which Noor wouldn't love. That's the bit I'd lose sleep over, honestly, more than the job.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to plan, if anyone actually starts.
I'd push the union for a **retraining** and pay protection deal while it has power, and write to our MP.
think: My qualification would **lose value** right after I finish training in 2029.
By 2031 I might be experienced enough to be **kept** for hands-on work until 2034.
do: Finish training and steer my last year toward **hands-on skills** like coils, implants and home visits.
Save **£200 a month** after my 2027 pay rise to reach three months' cushion.
Start a **diploma** in caring for older patients.
feel: A **constant worry**, less sharp than the two-year picture.
Aware the five years would **go quickly**.
S3.quote: I'd have a family medicine qualification that's worth less right after I get it.
fieldNote: He uses the five years to **choose** a path rather than grab one: older-patient care.
Sees a narrow chance to become one of the doctors **kept** for hands-on work.
The real cost is **family plans**: he'd delay a baby, which strains things with Noor.
First time he'd **write to an MP**, a step up from staff-room talk.

steps.text: Steer the last training year towards coils, implants and home visits
Save £200 a month after the 2027 pay rise
Write to the local MP asking for a plan for health workers
Delay trying for a baby until 2031 is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career stage away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. I'd want the union and the health trust building a plan together: who retrains, who gets protected, what patients get. I'd probably be the annoying one in branch meetings saying we should start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm in a decent spot. I'd have six or seven years as a full family doctor before AGI, and the touch side of the job lasts until about 2039. My skills would be solid by then, but I'd still have no savings to speak of unless I change something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish training, get my diploma in caring for older people, and start building savings slowly, aiming for six months by 2033. I'd use AI tools when the clinic brings them in, once they've proved themselves on the notes. And I'd think about taking on extra sessions at the care home on Mill Lane, because that work is hands-on and it pays a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. Like knowing a storm is coming next winter, and having time to fix the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to money. Why does that matter more to you than the AI part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the AI part I can't control, and money I can, a bit. My dad lost his job at the dye works when I was eleven and we had nothing to fall back on. I remember the electricity going off. I never want to be that close to the edge again, and right now I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a medical student who asked you about this future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the hands-on stuff properly, joint injections and examinations and sitting with dying people, because that's the part that lasts. And I'd tell them to save a little every month from day one, which I didn't do.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift and we'd be foolish to waste it.
I'd want the union and the health trust building a **joint plan** for staff and patients.
think: I'd have **six or seven years** as a full doctor before AGI arrives.
My skills would be solid, but my **savings** would still be close to nothing.
do: Finish training and the **older-patient diploma** by the end of the decade.
Build savings slowly toward **six months** by 2033.
Take extra **care home** sessions on Mill Lane for hands-on work and more pay.
feel: **Uneasy but okay**, like seeing next winter's storm with time to fix the roof.
S4.quote: My dad lost his job at the dye works when I was eleven and we had nothing to fall back on. I remember the electricity going off.
fieldNote: With ten years he expects his **own job** to hold, so worry drops to uneasy.
His fear of being broke comes from **childhood**: his dad's job loss and the power cut.
Plans are steady and practical: diploma, slow **savings**, care home sessions.
Would adopt AI tools once they've **proved themselves**, true to his steady nature.

steps.text: Finish training and an older-patient care diploma
Save steadily to reach six months of expenses by 2033
Take paid extra sessions at the Mill Lane care home
Use the clinic's AI note tools once they prove reliable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd be a trainee with no savings and no time. What would help is a guarantee that trainees finish their training, paid, whatever happens, and a hardship fund through the union. And some clear rules from government about what AI can decide in a clinic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the patients, and that's what I'd want on record. The people in Millbrook already wait three weeks to see us, and if an AI makes it faster, fine, but someone has to still be in the room when a man finds out his cancer is back. A good doctor is mostly someone who stays in the room.

headlineQuote: A good doctor is mostly someone who stays in the room.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** trainee family doctor at a public clinic in an old mill town.
He lives with his partner Noor, a teacher, with **three weeks** of savings and a student loan.
His fear of being broke goes back to his dad's **job loss** at the dye works.
He backs the **union** and rules, but would use AI tools once they prove themselves.
He moves from **uneasy** in the plateau to **alarmed** with AGI in two years, and settles back with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd still be a trainee with no savings and no time.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that trainees **finish training** on pay, plus a union **hardship fund**.
Clear government **rules** on what AI may decide in a clinic.
